job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**S. 2817 drafting review, text as amended October 6, 2026**

1. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel":** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel, so an operator could split recovery across several vessels, each under the cap. The bill doesn't aggregate tonnage by operator, affiliate, or project.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year" and "recovery":** The cap is annual with no cumulative or multi-year test, and "recovery" is undefined (lifted to deck, delivered to shore, or processed). Operators could pace extraction or choose a counting point that keeps them under the threshold.

3. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" and "200 meters":** "Other mineral resources" is undefined, so it's unclear whether crusts, sulfides, or sediment-based resources are covered. The 200-meter floor also leaves shallower-water activity outside the definition, which the drafters should confirm is intended.

4. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary" and "determines":** No criteria, procedure, notice, or hearing govern the designation of "comparable" activities. "The Secretary" is never identified, and §6 separately names the Secretary of State, so the reference is ambiguous. The standardless delegation is also vulnerable to nondelegation and arbitrary-and-capricious challenges.

5. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** Defining the term as a citizen or a state-chartered corporation leaves out LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and foreign-incorporated affiliates of U.S. firms. Corporate structuring alone could move operations outside the prohibition.

6. **§3(a), "in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere":** The prohibition reaches U.S. persons but not foreign-flagged vessels or foreign-incorporated operators working in other nations' zones or on the high seas. It also doesn't address mining in the ISA Area, and "in the United States" is undefined as to whether it covers the EEZ and continental shelf.

7. **§3(a), "engage in":** The term is undefined and doesn't clearly reach financing, insurance, chartering, equipment supply, processing, purchasing, or marketing. Those support activities could continue even if recovery stops.

8. **§3(a), no import or sales restriction:** The bill doesn't bar importing or selling minerals recovered abroad. Nodules mined under foreign authority could still enter U.S. supply chains.

9. **§3(b), "exploration license":** The exemption covers all mining under any pre-enactment exploration license, with no volume cap, duration limit, or requirement that the activity remain exploratory. DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.) distinguishes exploration licenses from commercial recovery permits, and the bill doesn't address the latter. Counsel should confirm how that distinction plays out here.

10. **§3(b), heading versus text:** The heading "Existing Operations" describes a test (operations underway) that differs from the text (a license issued). The bill also says nothing about renewal, amendment, transfer, or expansion of a pre-enactment license.

11. **§3(b), "before the date of enactment":** Using enactment as the cutoff creates an incentive to accelerate license issuance between introduction and enactment. A freeze keyed to the introduction date would close this gap.

12. **§3(c), "for the purpose of environmental assessment":** The exemption depends on a self-declared purpose, with no volume cap, approval requirement, time limit, reporting duty, or standard for genuineness. Commercial-scale recovery labeled as assessment would fall outside the ban, making this likely the largest gap in the bill.

13. **§2(3) and §4, covered vessel versus commercial mining:** Registration and reporting apply only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons "equipped for" recovery, but the prohibition applies by annual volume regardless of vessel size. An operator could mine at commercial volume with smaller vessels and avoid both registration and reporting.

14. **§2(3), "equipped for the recovery" and "vessel":** Neither term addresses autonomous systems, towed collectors, or platform-based systems. Recovery equipment could be split across units so that no single vessel meets the definition.

15. **§4(a), "operator":** The term is undefined and doesn't distinguish owner, operator, or charterer. The section also says nothing about foreign-flagged vessels and sets no registration deadline.

16. **§4(b), reporting content and oversight:** The quarterly report has no required content (tonnage, location, depth, processing), no public disclosure, and no NOAA duty to verify, audit, or review. It also doesn't cover §3(c) assessment activities, so the exempt category has no visibility.

17. **§4 and §5, no penalty for registry violations:** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or to file a report carries no stated consequence. The registry is effectively unenforceable beyond whatever general authority applies.

18. **§5(a), "for each day on which the violation occurs":** The bill doesn't say whether a continuing operation accrues per day, per voyage, or per vessel. The penalty is hard to calculate and easy to contest, and the bill sets no inflation adjustment or express limitations period.

19. **§5, no enforcement mechanism:** The bill names no enforcing agency and provides no administrative procedure, injunction authority, vessel detention or forfeiture, cease-and-desist power, or citizen suit. Enforcement would depend entirely on DOJ action.

20. **§5(a) versus §8, effective date:** §5(a) applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays the prohibition by 180 days. Read literally, conduct during that window might be penalized before §3 takes effect, which invites a fair-notice challenge.

21. **§5(b), "willfully":** The term is undefined, and the bill doesn't expressly address officer or director liability. Individuals who direct a violation may face no criminal exposure beyond what general principles provide.

22. **§6, "shall seek to negotiate":** The duty is only to try, with no consequence for failure, no reporting requirement, and no trigger for suspending or revisiting §3. "Equivalent to those in section 3" is undefined, so any agreement could fall short of the bill's standard.

23. **§7(a), "serious harm" and "finds by joint resolution":** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the bill doesn't clarify whether a joint resolution's finding alone lifts §3 or whether the resolution must also repeal or suspend it. A joint resolution is also subject to presentment and veto. The bill doesn't require NASEM to produce the report or fund it, and NASEM is not an agency, so the trigger may never occur.

24. **§7(a) versus §7(b), conflicting durations:** Subsection (a) keeps the prohibition in place until a joint resolution is adopted, but subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. After year 10, the ban lapses even if no finding was made, which makes the sunset the operative end date.

25. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The bill doesn't preserve pending enforcement actions, accrued penalties, or ongoing investigations after sunset. Defense counsel could argue that these lapse with the Act.

26. **General, no severability clause:** If a court strikes a provision such as the §2(1)(B) designation power, the bill has no fallback to keep the rest in force. That raises the risk that a single successful challenge disables the operative parts.

27. **General, relationship to DSHMRA and NOAA regulations:** The bill doesn't amend DSHMRA or state which regime controls, and existing NOAA rules (15 C.F.R. Part 970) could conflict with it. Counsel should confirm how the bill interacts with the current permitting framework.

---

**Notes for Thursday's markup**

- The highest-impact items are #12 (§3(c) assessment exemption), #9 and #10 (§3(b) license grandfathering), #13 (§2(3)/§4 vessel-size gap), and #24 (§7 duration conflict). These create the most concrete avenues for operations to continue.
- I worked from the text you provided only. I haven't seen the pre-amendment version or any CRS or committee analysis, so the October 6 manager's amendment may have resolved some of these points or introduced new ones.
- The DSHMRA references and the enforcement and limitations analysis (#18, #19, #27) should be checked by counsel before anything goes to lawmakers or staff.
